questions.question: What is the first priority when evaluating acute abdominal pain?
choices: Choose an antacid
Assess stability, perfusion, bleeding, dehydration, peritoneal signs, mental status, and emergency red flags
Order every possible laboratory test
Classify pain only by abdominal quadrant
questions.explanation: Acute abdominal assessment begins with stability. Hemodynamic compromise, peritonitis, major bleeding, obstruction, ischemia, sepsis, or ectopic pregnancy can require emergency evaluation.

questions.question: Why should pregnancy possibility be assessed early in a patient with reproductive potential and abdominal or pelvic symptoms?
choices: It is relevant only if the patient reports missed periods
It changes the differential, urgency, medication safety, and imaging choices
It replaces the abdominal examination
It makes all imaging contraindicated
questions.explanation: Pregnancy can change both the differential and care pathway. Pain or bleeding with a positive test requires attention to ectopic pregnancy and other complications.

questions.question: What is the generally appropriate sequence for a focused abdominal examination?
choices: Palpate, percuss, auscultate, inspect
Inspect, auscultate, percuss, palpate
Percuss, palpate, inspect, auscultate
Auscultate, palpate, inspect, percuss
questions.explanation: Inspection and auscultation precede palpation because palpation can increase discomfort and alter bowel sounds. Begin palpation away from maximal pain.

questions.question: Which presentation most strongly supports emergency evaluation for possible GI bleeding?
choices: Stable minor rectal bleeding without symptoms
Melena with tachycardia, dizziness, near-syncope, or hypotension
A remote history of hemorrhoids
One dark stool after a medication known to change stool color without other symptoms
questions.explanation: Melena with signs of reduced perfusion or significant blood loss can represent an emergency. Assess hemodynamics and arrange urgent evaluation.

questions.question: A patient has new jaundice, fever, right-upper-quadrant pain, and confusion. What is the best FNP response?
choices: Wait several weeks for routine liver tests
Recognize a potentially serious hepatobiliary or hepatic process and arrange urgent evaluation
Assume a supplement is the sole cause
Treat only with an antiemetic
questions.explanation: Jaundice with systemic symptoms, RUQ pain, altered mental status, bleeding, hypotension, or decompensation features requires urgent assessment.

questions.question: Which statement about a benign-appearing abdominal examination is most accurate?
choices: It excludes appendicitis, ectopic pregnancy, ischemia, and obstruction
It must be interpreted with time course, risk, symptoms, vital signs, and reassessment
It proves the cause is functional
It makes pregnancy testing unnecessary
questions.explanation: A normal or mildly abnormal early examination may not exclude evolving or high-consequence disease. Integrate the entire presentation.

questions.question: A patient has sudden severe abdominal pain that seems disproportionate to initial examination findings and has atrial fibrillation. What is the safest principle?
choices: Assume simple gastroenteritis
Consider high-consequence vascular and surgical causes and arrange urgent emergency evaluation
Repeat outpatient antiemetics until pain improves
Schedule routine imaging next month
questions.explanation: Severe pain out of proportion with vascular risk can raise concern for mesenteric ischemia and other emergencies; outpatient reassurance is unsafe.

questions.question: What is the best role for abdominal imaging?
choices: It replaces emergency transfer in unstable patients
It answers a specific clinical question and is selected based on suspected condition, stability, pregnancy context, and local protocol
CT is always the first test for every abdominal complaint
Imaging is unnecessary if pain is severe
questions.explanation: Imaging is targeted. Ultrasound, CT, MRI, and other studies have different roles; instability requires emergency stabilization and disposition first.

questions.question: Why should medication reconciliation be part of an abdominal/GI assessment?
choices: Medications cannot affect GI symptoms
NSAIDs, anticoagulants, GLP-1/GIP-GLP-1 drugs, alcohol, supplements, and other agents can alter bleeding, liver, pancreatic, bowel, and dehydration risk
Only antibiotics matter
The medication list is unrelated to diagnostic reasoning
questions.explanation: Medication and substance exposure can change the differential and safety plan. Verify what the patient actually takes, including OTC products and supplements.

questions.question: What is essential in a safe outpatient abdominal plan?
choices: Vague advice to return if worse
Specific return precautions, result-follow-up ownership, and reassessment for worsening/localizing pain, bleeding, fever, vomiting, jaundice, or inability to hydrate
Assuming one normal test ends follow-up
Avoiding discussion of uncertainty
questions.explanation: GI and abdominal illness can evolve. Clear safety-netting and result tracking reduce missed or delayed diagnosis.
